solution: The key observation is that on a binary array a forward bubble pass is exactly 'delete the first 1 and append a 1 at the end', and a reverse bubble pass is exactly 'delete the last 0 and prepend a 0 at the front'. Consequently the array is always of the form 0^A + a[l..r] + 1^B for a window [l, r] of the original array, where l only ever increases and r only ever decreases: a forward pass advances l past the first 1 in the window (its leading zeros join the 0 block, the 1 joins the 1 block), and a reverse pass retracts r before the last 0. The padding blocks contribute nothing, so the answer at every step is simply the inversion count of the current window, and each pass decreases it by the number of zeros (resp. ones) remaining in the shrunk window, read off prefix sums of zeros and ones. With next-one and previous-zero jump tables the two pointers move monotonically, giving O(n) time and memory per test; once the window loses all its 0s or all its 1s the array is sorted and every later answer is 0. Verified against all seven samples and 30000 randomized tests against a direct simulation.

notes: On the inversion-count question from the assignment: the quantity asked for is genuinely the inversion count, reported n+1 times, and the incremental update is derived from the inversion identity for binary arrays (each 1 contributes the number of 0s to its right). But it is not a merge-sort / BIT inversion-counting problem, because for a binary array the count is a prefix-sum expression; the real work is characterizing what one bubble pass does. Labelled inversion-count at 0.8 for that reason rather than 0.95. Judge tags list 'data structures', but no data structure beyond prefix arrays is needed. Rating is None (contest unrated at extraction time); Div. 3 F with n up to 5*10^5 and a 3s limit, so an O(n) or O(n log n) solution is intended.
